Night Sweats Waking Me Up Every Night: What Are My Options?

By Marian Grout, founder of 3:17 · Updated October 25, 2026

Short answer

There isn't one answer. Options include bedroom and bedding changes, keeping a diary of your nights, and asking a clinician about hormone therapy, non-hormonal prescriptions or CBT. The Menopause Society describes hormone therapy as the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and recommends several nonhormone options, so the choice is personal.

You fall asleep fine. Then somewhere in the small hours you're awake, the sheet is damp, your heart is thumping, and you're peeling off a layer you swear you didn't need when you went to bed. Then comes the second problem: lying there, wide awake, doing sums about how many hours are left. If you're searching "night sweats waking me up every night, what helps?", I've been there, and I'm sorry. I'm Marian, and I started 3:17 because of nights exactly like these.

This article is a calm, balanced walk-through of the options women often ask about. It's not a quick fix list, and there's no single right answer. What I learned is that I wanted to make these decisions with someone who knows my health history.

What are night sweats, and why do they keep waking me up?

Vasomotor symptoms, the term researchers use, include hot flashes and night sweats.[3]

In the large SWAN study, among women with frequent hot flashes or night sweats (on 6 or more days in a two-week period), the median total duration was 7.4 years.[3] I'm sharing that as context, not a prediction about you. What I took from it is that if your nights are rough, you're not being dramatic, and it's reasonable to want a plan rather than just waiting it out.

I'm not a clinician, so I can't tell you exactly what is behind your nights. If you want answers about your own situation, a clinician is the person I'd go to.

Can changing my bedroom and bedding make nights easier?

These are the things I tried first, because they're in my own hands and don't need a prescription. I'm not citing a study for any of them. They're simply practical comfort ideas from my own experience and from other women I've talked to, and they won't suit everyone. Here's what you could try:

  • A cooler, well-ventilated bedroom. A fan, a cracked window or a lower thermostat setting.
  • Layered bedding. A light duvet plus a throw you can kick off, rather than one heavy cover.
  • Breathable fabrics. Some women like cotton, linen or bamboo sheets and nightwear instead of synthetics.
  • A spare set of pyjamas and a towel by the bed. If you wake damp, you can change quickly and go back to bed without a big production.
  • A glass of water within reach.

What I personally found is that preparing for a bad night took some of the dread out of it, even on the nights it didn't change what happened.

Is it worth keeping a diary of my nights?

I kept a simple diary for a while, jotting down a few things I was curious about, like what I'd had to drink in the evening, whether I'd eaten late, how my day had gone and how warm the room was. Sometimes I spotted a pattern and sometimes I didn't, and either was fine.

If you're curious, try it for two to four weeks. Jot down:

  • what time you woke and how sweaty you felt, on a scale you make up (1 to 5 is fine)
  • what you ate and drank in the evening
  • what the bedroom temperature was like
  • how stressed or wound-up you felt

This isn't about blaming yourself. I found that having notes to hand made it easier to describe my nights when I talked to a clinician.

What does The Menopause Society say about hormone therapy?

Hormone therapy is an option many people have heard of, and it comes with a lot of nuance, so it's worth reading what the professional bodies actually say.

The Menopause Society describes hormone therapy as the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms.[1] The same position statement says that for women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, and without contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favorable for treating bothersome vasomotor symptoms.[1] The benefit-risk ratio appears less favorable for women who initiate hormone therapy more than 10 years from menopause onset or who are older than 60.[1]

There's an important caveat that I think often gets lost in headlines. The risks of hormone therapy differ depending on type, dose, duration, route of administration, timing of initiation and whether a progestogen is used.[1] That's a lot of variables, which is why I'd want to work through them with a clinician who knows my age, my history, my family history and my preferences.

That's why I see it as a conversation with a clinician rather than a default. If you have concerns, bring them. A good appointment includes your worries, not just your symptoms.

What if I can't or don't want to take hormones?

Maybe that's you, whether because of your medical history, a personal preference or simply wanting to explore other routes first. The Menopause Society has published a separate position statement on nonhormone options.

The Menopause Society's 2023 nonhormone position statement recommends cognitive behavioral therapy, clinical hypnosis, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant for vasomotor symptoms.[2] If a prescription option interests you, I'd want to talk it through with a clinician, alongside my own health history and any other medicines I take.

I'll be honest that I'm not a clinician and I'm not going to rank these for you. What I can say is that the list above comes from a professional society's position statement, and it's a good thing to print or screenshot and bring to your appointment.

Is CBT worth asking about for the sleep I'm losing?

CBT sounds like a strange suggestion when the problem feels so physical, so I understand the raised eyebrow. A few things are worth separating out.

First, cognitive behavioral therapy appears on The Menopause Society's list of recommended nonhormone options for vasomotor symptoms, as above.[2]

Second, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends multicomponent CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) for adults with chronic insomnia disorder.[4] That guideline is for adults generally, not only women in menopause.

Third, there's research in women like us. In a randomized trial of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with vasomotor symptoms and insomnia, women assigned to telephone-based CBT-I had greater improvement in insomnia severity than women assigned to menopause education.[5]

For me, broken sleep became its own worry, with the dread of bedtime, the clock-watching and the 3 a.m. spiral. If that sounds familiar, I'd ask a clinician whether CBT-I is something they offer or can point me towards, including what's available near me or online.

What about supplements and the other things I keep seeing online?

If you search for night sweats, you'll see a lot of confident promises, many of them attached to something you can buy. I'm not going to point you to a supplement here. Personally, I'd ask a clinician or pharmacist before taking one, and I'd bring a list of any other medicines I take.

That goes for me and for 3:17 too. I'd rather you read the position statements above than take my word, or anyone's marketing, for how to approach your nights.

When should I talk to a clinician?

For me, the moment to book an appointment was when night sweats were happening regularly and getting in the way of my sleep, mood and days. If anything is new, worrying or you're simply unsure what's going on, that's a good reason to talk to a clinician too.

Here's what I'd bring:

  • your diary, even if it's only a week or two
  • a list of what you've already tried and how the nights felt afterwards
  • a list of all your medicines and supplements
  • your questions, such as "What are my options if I'd rather not take hormones?" or "Could CBT-I be offered to me?"
  • what matters most to you, whether that's sleep, safety, avoiding certain medicines or simply being heard

You're allowed to ask for a second opinion if you don't feel listened to.

So where does that leave me?

There isn't one answer, and I'd be wary of anyone who says there is. There are practical things you can try tonight, a diary you can keep, and a set of options from hormone therapy through non-hormonal prescriptions to CBT that professional societies describe, and that deserve a proper conversation with someone who knows you. You don't have to put up with this on your own.

Questions women ask

Are night sweats the same as hot flashes?

Hot flashes and night sweats are both included under the term vasomotor symptoms. If mine were disrupting my sleep, I'd describe the pattern to a clinician.

How long do night sweats last?

In the large SWAN study, among women with frequent hot flashes or night sweats (on 6 or more days in a two-week period), the median total duration was 7.4 years. I share that as context, not as a prediction for any one person.

Is hormone therapy my only option?

No. The Menopause Society's 2023 nonhormone position statement recommends cognitive behavioral therapy, clinical hypnosis, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant for vasomotor symptoms. I'd talk through with a clinician which, if any, fits my situation.

Is hormone therapy safe for me?

The Menopause Society's 2022 statement says the risks of hormone therapy differ depending on type, dose, duration, route of administration, timing of initiation and whether a progestogen is used. That is why I'd want to discuss it individually with a clinician.

Is CBT only for insomnia?

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends multicomponent CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) for adults with chronic insomnia disorder. The Menopause Society's nonhormone statement also lists cognitive behavioral therapy among its recommended options for vasomotor symptoms.

Should I take a supplement for night sweats?

I'm not able to recommend one here. Personally, I'd check with a clinician or pharmacist before starting any supplement, and I'd bring a list of my other medicines.
